statement: The potential of a point current source I in an infinite homogeneous conductor of conductivity σ is Φ = I / (4πσr) (Malmivuo & Plonsey eq. 8.7).
sources: Malmivuo J, Plonsey R (1995). Bioelectromagnetism: Principles and Applications of Bioelectric and Biomagnetic Fields. Oxford University Press Ch. 7 (quasistatic conditions), Ch. 8 (source–field models, eqs 8.7 and 8.15), Ch. 13 (EEG) https://www.bem.fi/book/

statement: In rat hippocampal CA1 in vivo, extracellular spikes recorded within 50 µm of the soma are ≥ 60 µV (the largest units ~600 µV).
sources: Henze DA, Borhegyi Z, Csicsvari J, Mamiya A, Harris KD, Buzsáki G (2000). Intracellular features predicted by extracellular recordings in the hippocampus in vivo. Journal of Neurophysiology 84(1):390–400 doi:10.1152/jn.2000.84.1.390

statement: Extracellular potentials from multiple current sinks and sources combine linearly by superposition; all volume conductors in bioelectricity are treated as linear.
sources: Buzsáki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C (2012). The origin of extracellular fields and currents — EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes. Nature Reviews Neuroscience 13(6):407–420 doi:10.1038/nrn3241

Malmivuo J, Plonsey R (1995). Bioelectromagnetism: Principles and Applications of Bioelectric and Biomagnetic Fields. Oxford University Press Ch. 7 (quasistatic conditions), Ch. 8 (source–field models, eqs 8.7 and 8.15), Ch. 13 (EEG) https://www.bem.fi/book/

statement: With simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG in 16 patients, intracranial spikes involving < 6 cm² of cortex were never seen on the scalp, only 10% of spikes with < 10 cm² produced scalp spikes, and 90% of spikes with > 10 cm² did; synchronous activation of 10–20 cm² of gyral cortex was common.
sources: Tao JX, Ray A, Hawes-Ebersole S, Ebersole JS (2005). Intracranial EEG substrates of scalp EEG interictal spikes. Epilepsia 46(5):669–676 doi:10.1111/j.1528-1167.2005.11404.x
Nunez PL, Nunez MD, Srinivasan R (2019). Multi-scale neural sources of EEG: genuine, equivalent, and representative. A tutorial review. Brain Topography 32(2):193–214 doi:10.1007/s10548-019-00701-3
Buzsáki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C (2012). The origin of extracellular fields and currents — EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes. Nature Reviews Neuroscience 13(6):407–420 doi:10.1038/nrn3241

statement: Human cerebrospinal fluid conductivity measured in 7 patients is 1.79 S/m at 37 °C (1.45 S/m at 25 °C) across 10 Hz–10 kHz; the meta-analytic weighted mean is 1.71 S/m.
sources: Baumann SB, Wozny DR, Kelly SK, Meno FM (1997). The electrical conductivity of human cerebrospinal fluid at body temperature. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering 44(3):220–223 doi:10.1109/10.554770
McCann H, Pisano G, Beltrachini L (2019). Variation in reported human head tissue electrical conductivity values. Brain Topography 32(5):825–858 doi:10.1007/s10548-019-00710-2

statement: The classical four-sphere model uses a 1 mm CSF layer (radii 8.0 and 8.1 cm); the occipital CSF layer thins by about 30% when a subject moves from prone to supine, raising occipital EEG power for spatially incoherent activity by about 80% on average.
sources: Nunez PL, Nunez MD, Srinivasan R (2019). Multi-scale neural sources of EEG: genuine, equivalent, and representative. A tutorial review. Brain Topography 32(2):193–214 doi:10.1007/s10548-019-00701-3
Rice JK, Rorden C, Little JS, Parra LC (2013). Subject position affects EEG magnitudes. NeuroImage 64:476–484 doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2012.09.041

statement: Scalp EEG amplitudes are of the order of 10–100 µV.
sources: Chi YM, Jung T-P, Cauwenberghs G (2010). Dry-contact and noncontact biopotential electrodes: methodological review. IEEE Reviews in Biomedical Engineering 3:106–119 doi:10.1109/RBME.2010.2084078

Malmivuo J, Plonsey R (1995). Bioelectromagnetism: Principles and Applications of Bioelectric and Biomagnetic Fields. Oxford University Press Ch. 7 (quasistatic conditions), Ch. 8 (source–field models, eqs 8.7 and 8.15), Ch. 13 (EEG) https://www.bem.fi/book/

statement: A common-mode rejection ratio of 80–90 dB is customary for differential biopotential amplifiers; a driven-right-leg circuit usually reduces common-mode voltage by a further 10–50 dB; 1–10 µV peak-to-peak of interference is considered acceptable.
sources: Metting van Rijn AC, Peper A, Grimbergen CA (1990). High-quality recording of bioelectric events. Part 1: Interference reduction, theory and practice. Medical & Biological Engineering & Computing 28(5):389–397 doi:10.1007/BF02441961

statement: The traditional way to obtain low-noise contact is to abrade the skin to a contact resistance of 5–10 kΩ; historically EEG practice required < 5 kΩ, and unabraded saline-sponge electrodes measure about 10 kΩ.
sources: Chi YM, Jung T-P, Cauwenberghs G (2010). Dry-contact and noncontact biopotential electrodes: methodological review. IEEE Reviews in Biomedical Engineering 3:106–119 doi:10.1109/RBME.2010.2084078
Ferree TC, Luu P, Russell GS, Tucker DM (2001). Scalp electrode impedance, infection risk, and EEG data quality. Clinical Neurophysiology 112(3):536–544 doi:10.1016/S1388-2457(00)00533-2

statement: With a high-input-impedance active-electrode system, sites left at their natural 10–190 kΩ needed about 35 trials to reach 80% power for a P3 effect versus about 12 trials for sites abraded to < 5 kΩ; the extra noise was mainly below 5 Hz (skin potentials) and worse in a warm, humid room.
sources: Kappenman ES, Luck SJ (2010). The effects of electrode impedance on data quality and statistical significance in ERP recordings. Psychophysiology 47(5):888–904 doi:10.1111/j.1469-8986.2010.01009.x

statement: Scalp spatial power spectra measured with a 3 mm-pitch linear array peak at 0.1–0.4 cycles/cm (wavelengths 2.5–10 cm), suggesting ~1 cm optimal spacing; a finite-element study by the same group argues for a practical Nyquist of 3 cycles/cm (3 mm spacing), a minority view.
sources: Freeman WJ, Holmes MD, Burke BC, Vanhatalo S (2003). Spatial spectra of scalp EEG and EMG from awake humans. Clinical Neurophysiology 114(6):1053–1068 doi:10.1016/S1388-2457(03)00045-2

Ramon C, Freeman WJ, Holmes M, Ishimaru A, Haueisen J, Schimpf PH, Rezvanian E (2009). Similarities between simulated spatial spectra of scalp EEG, MEG and structural MRI. Brain Topography 22(3):191–196 doi:10.1007/s10548-009-0104-7

statement: People learned two-dimensional cursor control from scalp sensorimotor rhythms, and four adults learned simultaneous control of three independent EEG signals (one per dimension, from 3–4 electrodes), reaching targets in a virtual cube in 56–93% of trials; three is the most independent volitional dimensions demonstrated this way.
sources: Wolpaw JR, McFarland DJ (2004). Control of a two-dimensional movement signal by a noninvasive brain–computer interface in humans. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 101(51):17849–17854 doi:10.1073/pnas.0403504101
McFarland DJ, Sarnacki WA, Wolpaw JR (2010). Electroencephalographic (EEG) control of three-dimensional movement. Journal of Neural Engineering 7(3):036007 doi:10.1088/1741-2560/7/3/036007
